g-relative-08.reason: whose + (adjectives) + resume + lists: the finalist's resume. who / whom / who's: none can sit before a noun phrase 'recently updated and unusually detailed resume' that is itself the subject of 'lists'. 'who recently updated' is locally readable as a verb, but then 'and unusually detailed resume lists' has no grammar. 'who's' (who has / who is) fails the same way. No second reading in BrE or AmE.
g-relative-08.ldbs: L yes (who / who's read as 'who recently updated' inside the 4-word window); D yes but barely (the noun resume is the 5th word after the gap, and lists is further); B no (nobody confidently believes who's); S no. Medium at the low end. It is basically the whose + noun recognition test with two premodifiers pushing the noun out.
g-relative-08.why: Medium: L and D pass (the noun resume sits just outside the window); B and S fail, since whose + noun is routine and who's is a homophone gimmick, not a trap good students believe.
g-relative-08.editorNote: Same design as g-relative-15 (whose + premodified noun, who's as a homophone distractor). See overall.

g-relative-10.reason: Sentential non-defining 'which' (the whole event of the caterer withdrawing) + is exactly what ... feared. what: 'the gala, what is exactly what' is not standard in any formal register (what cannot follow a comma as a relative). it / that: 'the gala, it/that is exactly what the organizers had feared' is grammatical only as a new independent clause, so after a comma it is a comma splice. Formal editors would correct it, so it is not defensible. NOTE for the fixer: the exclusion of it and that rests entirely on the single comma plus the absence of a conjunction (and that is ...); with a semicolon, a dash or 'and' both would be fine. 'that' as a non-defining relative is also non-standard, so the exclusion of that is double.
g-relative-10.ldbs: L arguable (it / that read fine as a spliced clause locally); D no (the deciding element, the comma, is adjacent to the gap, and which after a comma is the textbook sentential relative); B weak (good students know comma + which); S no.
g-relative-10.why: Easy: D fails; the deciding cue is the comma directly in front of the gap, and this is the classic 'which refers to the whole clause' pattern.
g-relative-10.fix: Not required for accuracy. If it needs to go up: make the sentential reading less obvious, for example put an adverbial between the comma and the gap or make the clause after the gap longer, and replace what with a form that tempts more.
g-relative-10.editorNote: Exclusion of it and that depends on the comma/comma splice only. Same design as g-relative-23 (sentential which vs who / what / that after a comma); one of the two should be re-designed.

g-relative-15.reason: whose combined enrollment: the enrollment of the three campuses (whose with an inanimate antecedent is standard formal English). which: 'which combined enrollment has doubled' leaves 'has doubled' without a subject (combined would have to be a verb, and then enrollment is its object). of which: 'of which combined enrollment' is not grammatical (it would have to be 'the combined enrollment of which'). who's: = who is / who has; who is wrong for an inanimate antecedent and 'who's combined enrollment' is not grammatical.
g-relative-15.ldbs: L weak (which reads as which + verb 'combined' only if you ignore has doubled); D no (enrollment and has doubled both sit within 4 words after the gap); B weak (of which is a real relative form, but not in this position); S no.
g-relative-15.why: Easy: D fails; the noun enrollment follows immediately and has doubled sits inside the window, so whose + noun is visible at a glance.
g-relative-15.fix: Not required. To harden: put a prepositional phrase or a second adjective between the gap and the noun and move the verb out of the window, or test 'of which' vs 'whose' directly by adding the noun after of which in a second item. Avoid a second whose item next to g-relative-08.
g-relative-15.editorNote: Same design as g-relative-08 (whose + noun with premodifier, who's as the weakest distractor). Both the same type of trap; 15 is easier than 08.

g-relative-17.reason: Three proposals, none met the ceiling, so a second round was announced. both / neither / either of which all need exactly two referents; with three proposals they are wrong. 'neither of which' used for three is not standard in formal writing. Independently, both of which met the ceiling contradicts 'a second round of tenders was therefore announced', and either of which met does not fit three and gives a weak result. No second answer.
g-relative-17.ldbs: L yes (neither of which met reads perfectly well inside the window and even fits the second-round result); D yes (three is about 13 words before the gap); B moderate (neither/none is a known trap, and the neither-for-two rule is one that some good students apply loosely); S no.
g-relative-17.why: Medium: L and D pass, but B is only moderate; the clue is the numeral three, a plain word, and neither/none is a rule most good students know.
g-relative-17.editorNote: Three of the four options fail on the same single cue (the number three); one item is therefore partly a 3-vs-1 elimination. Acceptable.

g-relative-21.reason: Reduced active relative: technicians performing the calibration ... have been reporting (main verb). performed: as a finite past tense it makes 'Technicians performed ..., have been reporting', two finite verbs with no conjunction; as a past participle (reduced passive) it would need a by-agent and the technicians do the calibrating. perform: same two-verb problem (a present-tense reading is also incoherent with the main verb). being performed: passive, so the technicians would be the thing being performed. No second answer.
g-relative-21.ldbs: L yes (performed and perform read as a full clause inside the window); D yes (the main verb have been reporting is about 18 words later, after an inserted most of them ... phrase); B yes (performed as a plain simple past is a form good students first accept); S yes (find the main verb first, then see that the gap needs a modifier). Hard, but at the low end of hard, since the object after the gap and the long interruption make the main verb easy to find.
g-relative-21.why: Hard by the rubric: L, D and S pass (and B for performed); the main verb appears only after the inserted most of them with ... phrase.
g-relative-21.editorNote: This is a participle (reduced relative) item, matching the 1.3 participle design, not a relative-pronoun item. Fine, because it varies the group.

g-relative-22.reason: who is the subject of 'will oversee'; 'the board believes' is an insertion. whom: overcorrection (whom as the subject of a finite verb), so not defensible (4.2). that: 'The head of the program, that the board believes will oversee' puts that after a comma in a non-defining clause about a person; wrong in formal BrE and AmE. whose: needs a noun next, but 'the board' follows and does not belong to the head. NOTE: the exclusion of that depends on the commas (non-defining); without the commas, 'The head of the program that the board believes will oversee' would be acceptable.
g-relative-22.ldbs: L yes (whom the board believes is fully natural inside the window); D yes but marginal (will oversee, the verb with no subject, is just outside; 'believes will' is at the edge); B yes (whom is the classic overcorrection that good students deliberately choose); S yes (remove the insertion to find the subject slot).
g-relative-22.why: Hard: L, D, B and S all pass (the textbook who/whom + believes insertion), though the D cue sits right at the edge of the window.
g-relative-22.editorNote: Same frame as g-relative-25 (title noun subject + comma + relative + insertion + comma-bounded clause, then 'has/is expected to ...'). Redesign one of them.

g-relative-23.reason: which = sentential relative referring to the whole act of releasing the schedule without consulting; led to confusion. who: 'the shift supervisors, who led to confusion' is grammatical, but 'lead to' with a person subject is unidiomatic, and the reading needs a premise the sentence does not give (that the supervisors themselves caused the confusion, which is at odds with the point that they were not consulted). Not defensible, but it is the near-miss the brief asked about. what: 'what led to' cannot follow an antecedent after a comma. that: non-defining that after a comma is not standard, and it is also a comma splice reading. Exclusion of that/what rests on punctuation + standard usage.
g-relative-23.ldbs: L yes (who after a plural person noun is fine inside the window); D no/weak (led to confusion sits next to the gap; what rules out who is the meaning of the first clause, not a distant word); B yes (people after the noun phrase supervisors reflexively pick who: antecedent proximity); S yes (the antecedent is the whole clause, not the nearest noun). Medium because D is not met.
g-relative-23.why: Medium: L and B pass (who after supervisors is the pull), S too, but D fails since the deciding meaning is in the adjacent predicate 'led to confusion'.
g-relative-23.fix: Make who impossible rather than odd: change the predicate to something only a clause can be, for example '..., ______ proved a costly oversight once the first trucks arrived on Monday and confusion spread across the loading dock.' (who proved a costly oversight cannot refer to supervisors). Alternatively 'which was a lapse that led to ...'. Also consider moving the antecedent so that supervisors is not the nearest noun.
g-relative-23.editorNote: shouldFix: the who option is grammatical-but-odd and needs an unstated assumption (supervisors caused the confusion), so it is not ambiguous under 4.2, but a skeptical editor could argue it. Same design as g-relative-10.

g-relative-24.reason: to whose attention the discrepancy had been brought (bring X to Y's attention, with the preposition pied-piped). whose: 'the manager whose attention the discrepancy had first been brought in January' lacks the to that 'be brought' needs; no stranded to is available in the stem. to whom: 'to whom attention the discrepancy ...' leaves attention without a determiner or role and is ungrammatical. whom: 'whom attention the discrepancy' is ungrammatical. No second reading.
g-relative-24.ldbs: L yes (whose attention the discrepancy reads smoothly in the window); D yes (the missing to is only exposed by had first been brought, which is outside the 4-word window); B yes (whose + noun is a form good students trust and the pied-piped to whose is the less familiar form); S yes (rebuild the relative clause: the discrepancy had been brought to X's attention).
g-relative-24.why: Hard: L, D, B and S all pass; whose attention looks right until you rebuild the clause and notice that 'brought' needs to.
g-relative-24.editorNote: Slightly awkward 'named the regional manager' (named as the person responsible?) but acceptable. Options B and C both begin with to, so a quick eliminator can use that to cut to two. Fine.

g-relative-25.reason: The stem reads '____, according to the minutes of the March meeting, been pressing', so the gap must supply the auxiliary: 'who has, according to the minutes ..., been pressing'. who / whom / whose have no auxiliary, so 'been' is left without has/have and the clause is ungrammatical. Only C works.
g-relative-25.ldbs: L yes (who reads fine in the window); D yes (the missing auxiliary shows up at 'been', 9-10 words later, after the according-to insertion); B no (nobody holds a rule that makes who right here; the cue is mechanical); S marginal (read through the insertion to see that been needs an auxiliary). Strictly medium, since the S step is trivial once been is seen.
g-relative-25.why: Medium: L and D pass; B fails and S is trivial, so this tests noticing a missing auxiliary rather than a relative-pronoun rule.
g-relative-25.fix: Move the auxiliary out of the gap so the item tests a relative pronoun: '... The regional director, ______, according to the minutes of the March meeting, has been pressing the board ...' with who / whom / whose / that (answer who; whom is the overcorrection, that is excluded by the commas, whose by the missing noun). That also gives the item a real B. But then it duplicates g-relative-22, so change the frame (different noun, different insertion) or drop one of the two.
g-relative-25.editorNote: shouldFix on design: (1) the answer is the only two-word option and the only one carrying an auxiliary, a visible shape tell (style); (2) it mostly tests the auxiliary, not the pronoun; (3) same frame as g-relative-22.

shouldFix: g-relative-23: 'the shift supervisors, who led to confusion' is grammatical-but-odd, and needs an unstated assumption; not ambiguous under 4.2, but harden it (for example '... which/who proved a costly oversight ...') so who is impossible rather than odd.

g-relative-25: the answer is the only option containing an auxiliary ('who has') and the item tests a missing auxiliary rather than a relative pronoun; move 'has' out of the gap and use who / whom / whose / that, and change the frame because it duplicates g-relative-22.

g-relative-10 and g-relative-23: same design (sentential which after a comma against who / what / that / it); replace the design of one of them. In g-relative-10 the exclusion of it and that rests only on the comma.
g-relative-22 and g-relative-25: same frame (title noun subject + relative + insertion + comma-bounded clause); redesign one.
g-relative-08 and g-relative-15: same design (whose + noun, who's as homophone distractor); change one, preferably 15, which is easy.
overall: No item has a defensible second answer in formal BrE or AmE, so there is no mustFix. Bands: easy 2 (g-relative-10, g-relative-15), medium 4 (g-relative-08, g-relative-17, g-relative-23, g-relative-25), hard 3 (g-relative-21, g-relative-22, g-relative-24). Against the 5.2 target for grammar (easy at most 20%, medium 45 to 55%, hard at least 30%): hard is 33% (met), medium 44% (just under), easy 22% (just over). The hard items are the ones with a real B: whom as overcorrection after an insertion (22), whose vs the pied-piped 'to whose' (24), and the reduced relative with a long interruption (21; the lowest of the three hard items). The weak spots are the three easy-leaning items whose clue is adjacent to the gap (10, 15, 08) and the four duplicated designs (08/15 whose, 10/23 sentential which, 22/25 title-noun + insertion). 25 tests the auxiliary and not the pronoun. Exclusion of 'that' in 10, 22 and 23 depends on the commas (non-defining/comma splice), which is a legitimate trap, not an ambiguity, but note that the items rely on punctuation to do it.
